item.research_question: Is it possible to introduce short-range ordering (SRO) in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to simultaneously enhance both ultimate strength and ductility, and what microstructures and mechanisms are required?
item.processing_route: Hybrid Monte Carlo (MC) and Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations: MC site-occupancy swaps at 300 K and 1200 K using the Metropolis criterion, interchanged with MD relaxations (100 MC swaps followed by up to 100 MD relaxations per iteration) to optimize SRO; DFT calculations performed to validate cohesive energies.
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile deformation simulations at strain rates of 2 × 10^8 s^-1 and 2 × 10^7 s^-1, at temperatures of 300 K and 1200 K; initial sample size 8788 atoms with lattice constant 3.6 Å.
key_findings: The potential energy per atom decreased from -4.090 eV/atom (0 iterations) to -4.113 eV/atom (4 × 10^6 iterations), indicating energetically favorable SRO formation.
At 300 K, the ultimate stress increased from 3.4 GPa (no SRO) to 4.9 GPa (strong SRO), and ultimate strain increased from 6.0% to 9.6%.
SRO development led to the formation of three cluster types: FCC-preferred (FCCP), BCC-preferred (BCCP), and indifferent (IND) clusters.
FCCP clusters are primarily composed of Co (29 at%) and Ni (48 at%), while BCCP clusters are enriched in Fe (31 at%) and Pd (44 at%).
FCCP clusters withstand approximately 2 GPa/atom higher stresses than BCCP and IND clusters during deformation.
BCCP clusters undergo large plastic strain, acting as soft fillers, while FCCP clusters suffer relatively little plastic strain.
Strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations occurred in localized regions prior to the ultimate stress, driven by local compositional stability.
The presence of BCC-type structures prior to deformation was 2.4% for the 2 M sample and 3.0% for the 4 M sample, compared to 0% in the no-SRO sample.
item.mechanism: The SRO creates a pseudo-composite microstructure where indifferent (IND) clusters act as a matrix, FCC-preferred (FCCP) clusters serve as hard fillers to enhance strength, and BCC-preferred (BCCP) clusters act as soft fillers to increase ductility. Deformation involves strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations prior to the ultimate stress, which increases work hardening, followed by dislocation slip within the untransformed FCC phase.
item.limitations: The strain rates employed (2 × 10^8 s^-1) are very large compared with typical experiments, so the stress-strain curves should be interpreted as indicative of trends rather than quantitative values.
item.future_work: The authors suggest combining the SRO-based approach with larger-scale approaches (e.g., grain size, precipitates) to further optimize HEA mechanical response and exploring the effect of annealing temperature and grain boundaries on SRO and mechanical properties.
quotes: Our results show that this HEA is energetically favorable to undergo short-range ordering (SRO), and the SRO leads to a pseudo-composite microstructure, which surprisingly enhances both the ultimate strength and ductility.
The SRO-induced composite microstructure consists of three categories of clusters: face-center-cubic-preferred (FCCP) clusters, indifferent clusters, and body-center-cubic-preferred (BCCP) clusters.

The underlying mechanism responsible for the enhancement of both the ultimate strength and ductility in the HEA by SRO is described in terms of their mechanical responses of the three types of clusters: indifferent clusters play the role of a matrix, FCC-preferred clusters serve as hard fillers that enhance strength, and BCC-preferred clusters act as soft fillers that increase the HEA ductility.
